name: name-that-hash
why: Feed it a mystery hash and it guesses the algorithm, a neat dive into how digests are fingerprinted.

brief.what_it_is: Name-That-Hash is a command-line tool and Python module that identifies what type of hash a string is. You give it a hash such as 5f4dcc3b5aa765d61d8327deb882cf99 and it lists the likely algorithms, ranked by popularity, with a short summary of each. It can output JSON, and it can be imported as a Python module. A web app at nth.skerritt.blog does the same thing in a browser with no install.
brief.why_it_exists: The README asks, "Have you ever come across a hash such as 5f4dcc3b5aa765d61d8327deb882cf99 and wondered what type of hash that is?" It positions itself as a modern successor to HashID (last updated 2015) and Hash-Identifier (2011), and says it was heavily inspired by them.
brief.how_it_works: The README says the hash database began with HashID's roughly 3000 hashes but has been significantly modified. Matches are ranked by popularity so common hashes like NTLM appear above obscure ones like Skype. Each hash entry has a regex and a summary, and the default view also shows John the Ripper and HashCat mode information. The README says hashes are defined in name_that_hash/hashes.py and that each one is tested for both false and true positives.

brief.install_notes: Install with pip3 install name-that-hash, then run nth. The README also lists packages in REMnux, the Arch User Repository (python-name-that-hash), MacPorts, and Homebrew. No accounts, hardware, or extra runtime setup are mentioned. The README gives no separate first-run configuration steps. The web app needs no install.
brief.standout: Popularity ranking is the main difference from older tools, so NTLM is shown above Skype. Each hash also comes with a short usage summary, and the default output includes hashcat and John the Ripper modes. The author also says the tool is accessibility-focused, with a --accessible flag and colour choices made with a designer.
brief.status: The README calls it "a 2021 project" and refers to commits for the last update, but it shows no release date or last-commit date. The Discord, PyPI and packaging badges suggest it is still in use, but I could not confirm recent activity. Status is unknown from these pages.
brief.caveats: The homepage is a JavaScript app and shows only "You need to enable JavaScript to run this app" without JavaScript. The README gives no licence in the text I read. The README notes that --accessible hides the least-likely results, so a hash that falls in that group will not show. The tool identifies hash formats only; it cannot crack or verify a hash. The README says it removes non-hash formats such as base64 from its results.
